sections.html:
A Colorado landlord can hold no more than two months of rent as a security deposit, under C.R.S. 38-12-102.5. A few related limits go with it:

  • An extra pet deposit cannot be more than $300, and it must be refundable.
  • The landlord may deduct for unpaid rent, abandonment, unpaid utilities and repair or cleaning the tenant agreed to pay. Normal wear and tear is off limits.
  • A landlord who keeps any of the deposit must send a written statement giving the exact reasons and refund the rest. Missing the deadline forfeits the right to withhold anything.
  • A tenant cannot waive deposit rights, and a lease clause that tries to do so is unenforceable.

sections.h2: What happens to the deposit when the landlord sells
sections.html:
The deposit travels with the property. Under C.R.S. 38-12-103(4), when a rental changes hands the deposit goes to the new owner, or it goes back to the tenant after lawful deductions. The rule covers any change in ownership, including sale, assignment, death or receivership. An owner who sells a rented house cannot pocket the tenant's deposit and walk away.

That leaves two paths at closing:

  1. Hand the deposit to the buyer and write the amount into the sale contract so both sides agree on it.
  2. Return it to the tenant, with a written itemization of any deductions, if the tenant is leaving.

Tell the title company which path you are taking so the settlement statement shows the deposit correctly.

Every Colorado landlord warrants that a rental is fit to live in and must keep it that way for the whole tenancy. The warranty is in C.R.S. 38-12-503(1) and runs through the Part 5 statutes, which the legislature updated in 2024.

A breach has three parts: an uninhabitable condition, notice to the landlord, and a failure to begin or finish repairs. The statute sorts problems into two groups.

GroupExamples in the statute
Regular conditionsMold that materially affects health or safety, a substantial lack of working appliances, plumbing or gas not maintained, electrical systems not maintained, code violations
Conditions that materially interfere with life, health or safetyGas hazards, inadequate running or hot water, no electricity or hazardous wiring, no working exterior locks, rodent, pest or insect infestations

Tenants have duties too. They must keep the unit clean, safe and habitable, and a landlord is not responsible for problems the tenant caused through action, inaction or negligence.

sections.h2: How fast a landlord must respond to a repair notice
sections.html:
For a condition that materially interferes with life, health or safety, remedial action has to start within 24 hours of notice, under C.R.S. 38-12-503(2)(b). If the tenant asks, the landlord must also supply a comparable unit or a hotel room at no cost within 24 hours of the request. The landlord is presumed to have failed when such a condition persists seven calendar days after notice.

Work must continue until the problem is fully fixed within a reasonable time. The landlord has a defense when the tenant caused the delay by denying entry, refusing a reasonable alternative time or otherwise slowing the repairs.

If you may sell the rental, keep dated records of every repair notice and every response. A buyer will ask to see them.

sections.h2: What a tenant can do when repairs are not made
sections.html:
C.R.S. 38-12-507 lists several remedies.

  • Terminate the lease. If a condition is still unfixed after a reasonable time, the tenant can end the lease with 10 to 60 days of written notice, with a termination date at least 10 days out.
  • Terminate for a repeat problem. If the same condition returns within six months of being fixed, 10 days of written notice is enough.
  • Deduct repair costs from rent. This takes 10 days of written notice, or 48 hours for conditions that materially interfere with health or safety, plus a qualified professional and a chance for the landlord to fix it first.
  • Go to court. Actual and punitive damages, costs, reasonable attorney fees, injunctions, restraining orders and specific performance are all listed.

An owner planning to sell usually wants repairs finished before the first showing, not after a tenant has started down one of these paths.

A landlord may not punish a tenant for using habitability rights. Section 38-12-509 protects tenants who raise problems with the landlord, a third party or a government agency, or who join a tenants' organization. Retaliatory acts include:

  • Raising rent or decreasing services.
  • Ending or declining to renew a lease without the tenant's written consent.
  • Starting or threatening an eviction.
  • Charging a fee, cost or penalty.
  • Intimidation, threats, discrimination or harassment.

A tenant who proves retaliation can recover damages, attorney fees and costs, and may end the lease. Retaliation can also be raised as a defense in a possession case. The statute does not stop a landlord from serving a notice to terminate or vacate where Colorado law allows one.

Timing is the lesson for a seller. A termination notice served right after a repair complaint invites a retaliation argument.

sections.h2: Does a landlord need a reason to end a tenancy?
sections.html:
Yes. House Bill 24-1098 and C.R.S. 38-12-1303 require cause before a landlord serves a notice to terminate or files a possession action. As of November 2024 the legislature's summary counted 13 for-cause situations, including holding over after the lease ends, nonpayment, material lease violations and nuisance or negligent damage.

No-fault reasons are separate. One is that the landlord intends to stop renting and sell the home. The JDF 99 C form requires at least 90 days of notice for that route, with a move-out date after the lease term ends.

The form excludes tenants who have lived in the home less than a year, resident landlords of a single-family home, duplex or triplex, employer-provided housing, mobile home spaces and short-term rentals. Our eviction process page covers how those cases move through court.

Whether a buyer takes the house with a tenancy in place depends on the sale contract, the lease and these notice rules.

sections.h2: Selling a rental house for cash
sections.html:
A rental can be sold as is, with the tenant in place or after a lawful move-out. The law mostly decides how a tenancy ends, not whether the owner can sell.

Gather these items before you talk to a buyer:

  • The lease and any amendments.
  • The deposit amount and where it is held.
  • Written repair requests and records of what was done.
  • Any notice already served and the date it was served.

With those in hand, a buyer can price the house and the closing can be built around the tenant's situation. A buyer who takes the house occupied inherits the lease, so the lease terms, the rent and the deposit all belong in the contract. A buyer who wants it empty will need a lawful move-out first, and that sets the closing date.

We buy houses in Colorado as is, and we can walk through your lease and dates before you decide on a path. For legal questions, a Colorado attorney is the right call.

faqs.q: How much can a Colorado landlord charge for a security deposit?
faqs.a: No more than two months of rent. An additional pet deposit is limited to $300 and must be refundable.

faqs.q: What happens to the tenant's deposit if I sell the rental?
faqs.a: It must be given to the new owner or returned to the tenant after lawful deductions. The rule covers sale, assignment, death and receivership.

faqs.q: How quickly must a landlord start repairs on a dangerous condition?
faqs.a: Within 24 hours of notice for conditions that materially interfere with life, health or safety, such as gas hazards or no working exterior locks.

faqs.q: Can a tenant withhold rent for repairs?
faqs.a: Only by following the statute: 10 days of written notice, or 48 hours for health and safety conditions, using a qualified professional and giving the landlord a chance to fix it first.

faqs.q: Can I end a tenancy because I want to sell?
faqs.a: Yes, through the no-fault route, with at least 90 days of notice on form JDF 99 C. Tenants who have lived there less than a year and certain other groups are not covered by that form.
